newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sales tax rise won't have big economic impact -MOF.
newsitem.headline: Sales tax rise won't have big economic impact -MOF.

text.p: The rise in Japan's sales tax on Tuesday will not have a major impact on the overall economy, Vice finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa told a news conference on Monday.

He said the change in the tax to five percent from three percent had inevitably encouraged consumption before the rise and would dampen it afterwards, but added: "At the moment I don't think this impact would be so much as to cause distortion to the overall economy."

Low interest rates seem to have more impact on housing investments than the tax increase. For cars, the increase seems to have boosted demand before April 1, but the drop afterwards is likely to be gradual, he said.
Consumers are also becoming wiser in their purchases and are selecting only the goods they need to buy, Ogawa said.

Asked about Tokyo share prices at the end of the 1996/97 fiscal year on Tuesday, Ogawa said he believed that financial institutions and other companies have taken measures to cope with whatever level the share prices finished at on Tuesday.

Ogawa said it was important to come up with details on implementing a plan announced by the ministry earlier today to promote liquidity of collateralised land through securitisation, and the use of public money and deregulation to promote urban development.
He added that to facilitate securitisation of collateralised land, the ministry will consider reviewing the current tax system.

Asked to reiterate reasons for why Japan's big 20 banks will not fail, Ogawa said the banks were important to maintaining stability of the domestic financial system as well as the international financial system.
